prompt: The client asks: "Should we move our call center offshore?" Fact sheet: offshoring saves $5M a year; the move costs $8M once; satisfaction is expected to drop 10 points; each point of satisfaction lost costs $300k a year; our hurdle is a 3-year payback; the call center's $1M renovation finished last year. Which is the best recommendation?

options.text: Leave the call center where it is. A 10-point satisfaction drop cuts the $5M saving to $2M, so payback takes 4 years, beyond the hurdle.
options.feedback: Right. It leads with the answer and nets the satisfaction cost before computing payback.

options.text: Move offshore. $5M a year of savings pays back in under 2 years on the one-time $8M move, well inside the hurdle.
options.feedback: It ignores the $3M a year the satisfaction drop costs.

options.text: Keep the call center at home. We just spent $1M renovating it, and moving now would waste that.
options.feedback: The renovation is paid for either way. The satisfaction cost, which pushes payback past the hurdle, decides this.

options.text: Once the satisfaction drop costs $3M a year, the $5M saving falls to $2M and the $8M move takes 4 years to pay back. Offshoring isn't worth it.
options.feedback: The reasoning is right, but the answer comes last. Lead with the recommendation.

explanation: Full answer: Don't move the call center offshore. A 10-point satisfaction drop costs $3M a year, cutting the $5M saving to $2M, so the $8M move pays back in 4 years, beyond the 3-year hurdle. The main risk is that costs at home keep rising, so the next step is to look for savings through self-service and better scheduling. What would change the answer: a vendor that keeps the satisfaction drop to about 7 points or fewer.

irrelevant_facts: The call center's $1M renovation finished last year.
